network.overall_strategy: This is a connected, conditional reaction network containing 10 chemically distinct candidate pathways, not 10 experimentally established prebiotic syntheses. No end-to-end prebiotic synthesis of arginine is established by this network. Acetylene and HCN supply a four-carbon dinitrile skeleton; selective reduction would provide an aminoaldehyde for Strecker chain extension. Cyanamide supplies the guanidino carbon and two nitrogens. The pathways differ in when guanidination occurs and whether the alpha-amino-acid functionality is obtained through direct nitrile hydrolysis or a Bucherer-Bergs hydantoin branch. Hydantoins provide a chemically motivated opportunity to mask the alpha-amino group during side-chain guanidination. The shared, severe bottleneck is selective reduction of nitriles without over-reduction or cyclization; reactions rxn_003, rxn_004 and rxn_006 are explicitly speculative under the proposed geochemical conditions. Additional bottlenecks are aminoaldehyde cyclization, guanidination regioselectivity and survival during hydrolysis. Starting supplies of acetylene, HCN, ammonia, hydrogen, water, cyanamide and carbon dioxide are assumptions, not additional demonstrated synthesis pathways. All conditions exclude molecular oxygen, enzymes and modern activating reagents. Achiral chemistry predicts racemic arginine rather than selective L-arginine formation. Neutral formulas represent analytical species; solution protonation states depend on pH. Each environment_formed value identifies a representative formation environment, while reaction nodes specify alternative environments. The graph includes target-forming transformations, not every competing degradation product.

reactions.name: Copper-catalyzed hydrocyanation of acetylene

conditions.other: Anoxic, chloride-rich, sulfide-poor acidic pool; sustained acetylene and HCN delivery; shaded reaction zone.

reactions.mechanism: Copper-assisted addition of HCN across the acetylene triple bond produces acrylonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Acetylene hydrocyanation is an established synthetic reaction class and supplies the required unsaturated nitrile without an oxygen oxidant. Its operation in a natural pool is speculative: catalyst concentration, gas retention and competing acetylene oligomerization are unresolved. Dissolved copper is proposed only in a sulfide-poor setting because sulfide would sequester it.

reactions.name: Conjugate hydrocyanation to the four-carbon dinitrile
agents: Cyanide ions generated by HCN dissociation

conditions.other: Buffered pH approximately 8.5-10; concentrated but hydrated pool; limited residence time to reduce polymerization.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the beta carbon of acrylonitrile; proton transfer from HCN gives succinonitrile and regenerates cyanide.
reactions.reasoning: Conjugate cyanide addition to an activated alkene provides the correct unbranched C4 skeleton. The reaction class is chemically grounded, but useful production under these particular prebiotic conditions is not established. Acrylonitrile polymerization, hydrolysis and volatile-feedstock losses compete.

reactions.name: Selective hydrogenation of one succinonitrile nitrile group
agents: Native nickel-iron alloy surface, proposed awaruite-like catalyst

conditions.pressure: 50-200 bar total pressure; elevated hydrogen partial pressure
conditions.other: Anoxic rock-water pore; restricted catalyst contact and hydrogen exposure; rapid removal of any mono-reduced product.

reactions.mechanism: One nitrile undergoes hydrogenation through imine intermediates to a primary amine while the other nitrile remains intact.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and a shared major bottleneck. Nickel can catalyze nitrile hydrogenation, and native nickel-iron alloys can occur in serpentinizing systems, but selective accumulation of this mono-reduced product on a natural alloy is not established. Over-reduction to putrescine and cyclization to five-membered nitrogen compounds could dominate. This reaction supplies the first terminal amino group.

reactions.name: Partial reduction and hydrolysis to 4-aminobutanal
agents: Nickel-bearing metal surface, hypothetical partial-reduction catalyst

conditions.pressure: 50-150 bar total pressure; limited hydrogen activity
conditions.catalyst: Nickel-bearing surface; required partial-reduction selectivity unvalidated
conditions.other: Water-rich, mildly acidic pore; short catalyst residence followed by cooling and aldehyde trapping.

reactions.mechanism: Partial nitrile hydrogenation gives an aldimine, whose hydrolysis releases ammonia and the aldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and potentially prohibitive. Nitrile-to-aldehyde chemistry requires stopping reduction at the imine and favoring hydrolysis over further hydrogenation; no suitable native-mineral selectivity is established here. The aminoaldehyde also strongly favors cyclic imine formation. This edge must not be treated as a demonstrated hydrothermal source of the Strecker substrate.

reactions.name: Guanidination before aminoaldehyde formation

conditions.other: Concentrated, partially evaporated solution at pH approximately 9-10.5; residual water maintained; UV-shielded pore or sediment layer.

reactions.mechanism: The terminal primary amine adds to the cyanamide nitrile carbon, followed by proton transfers to form a substituted guanidine.
reactions.reasoning: Cyanamide-mediated amine guanidination is chemically established, but this substrate-specific prebiotic application is speculative. Performing it before alpha-amino-group installation avoids competition between two primary amines. Competing aminonitrile cyclization and cyanamide dimerization may prevent useful conversion.

reactions.name: Partial reduction of the guanidinated C4 nitrile
agents: Nickel-bearing metal surface, hypothetical partial-reduction catalyst

conditions.pressure: 50-150 bar total pressure; limited hydrogen activity
conditions.other: Mildly acidic, water-rich microenvironment; rapid product desorption and cooling.

reactions.mechanism: The terminal nitrile is partially hydrogenated to an imine and hydrolyzed to an aldehyde, with ammonia release.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative. This alternative attempts to reduce aminoaldehyde cyclization by installing the less nucleophilic guanidino group first. It still lacks a demonstrated prebiotic catalyst that stops at the aldehyde, and guanidine adsorption could poison the metal or alter selectivity. Preservation of the guanidino group is an additional requirement.

reactions.name: Guanidination of 4-aminobutanal

conditions.other: Concentrated cyanamide; pH approximately 8.5-10; freshly supplied aminoaldehyde; sheltered from direct UV.

reactions.mechanism: The open-chain terminal amine adds to cyanamide to generate a guanidino substituent while retaining the aldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate application of established guanidination chemistry. Early guanidination avoids alpha-versus-side-chain amine competition later, but open-chain 4-aminobutanal may be only a minor species because of rapid five-membered cyclic imine formation. Aldehyde condensation and cyanamide side reactions are unresolved competitors.

reactions.name: Strecker extension to ornithinonitrile

conditions.other: Ammonia- and cyanide-containing pool, pH approximately 8-9.5; continuous aminoaldehyde supply; attenuated UV in sediment pores.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine with the aldehyde; cyanide addition installs the new carbon and alpha-amino functionality.
reactions.reasoning: Strecker chemistry is well established for suitable aldehydes, but efficient reaction of this unstable aminoaldehyde under the stated conditions is speculative. Intramolecular imine formation can outcompete intermolecular ammonia capture, and the product can undergo additional cyclization. No enantioselectivity is supplied.

reactions.name: Strecker extension of 4-guanidinobutanal

conditions.other: Ammonia-rich, cyanide-containing water at pH approximately 8-9.5; guanidino group predominantly protonated.

reactions.mechanism: Aldehyde-imine formation followed by cyanide addition produces the alpha-aminonitrile carrying a preformed guanidino side chain.
reactions.reasoning: This is a chemically motivated but substrate-specific speculative Strecker reaction. Guanidinium protonation should reduce side-chain nucleophilicity relative to a free primary amine, potentially reducing cyclization. Actual aldehyde lifetime, competing condensation and aminonitrile yield remain unestablished.

reactions.name: Side-chain guanidination of ornithinonitrile

conditions.other: Concentrated cyanamide-containing solution; pH approximately 9-10.5; limited reaction time.

reactions.mechanism: The terminal side-chain amine adds to cyanamide, generating the guanidino group without changing the alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative with respect to regioselectivity. Both the alpha-amino and terminal amino groups can react; their different electronic environments do not establish exclusive side-chain guanidination. The graph represents the target-forming product channel, not a predicted selective synthesis. Intramolecular nitrile capture and multiple guanidination are competing reactions.

reactions.name: Hydration of ornithinonitrile to ornithinamide

conditions.other: Acidic water, approximately pH 1-3; moderate residence time followed by cooling if amide accumulation is desired.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-promoted water addition to the nitrile and proton transfers generate the primary carboxamide.
reactions.reasoning: Nitrile hydration is established chemistry, and protonation suppresses some amine-driven cyclization. Accumulating the amide rather than proceeding directly to the acid is a kinetic requirement, not an established environmental outcome. Product-specific rates and survival in acidic hydrothermal water require measurement.

reactions.name: Side-chain guanidination of ornithinamide

conditions.other: Cooling and pH adjustment after nitrile hydration; pH approximately 9-10.5; partial evaporative concentration.

reactions.mechanism: The terminal amino group adds to cyanamide to form argininamide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific application of cyanamide guanidination. Converting the nitrile to an amide changes electrophilicity and cyclization opportunities, making this a distinct chemical ordering. It does not protect the alpha-amino group, so wrong-site and double guanidination remain serious limitations.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of ornithinamide to ornithine

conditions.other: Acidic pore water, approximately pH 1-3; prolonged residence followed by cooling.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalyzed carboxamide hydrolysis produces the amino acid and ammonia, predominantly present as ammonium at the reaction pH.
reactions.reasoning: Amide-to-acid hydrolysis is chemically well founded and completes the conventional Strecker sequence. The proposed setting supplies heat and acidity without oxygen or enzymes. Whether hydrolysis outpaces competing degradation at naturally attainable acid concentrations is uncertain.

reactions.name: Terminal guanidination of ornithine

conditions.other: Concentrated solution at pH approximately 9-10.5; residual water during evaporation; protection from direct UV.

reactions.mechanism: Addition of the ornithine side-chain amino group to cyanamide gives the arginine guanidino group.
reactions.reasoning: Cyanamide is a chemically credible guanyl donor, but selective conversion of unprotected ornithine under these geochemical conditions is not established here. Alpha-amino guanidination, multiple guanidination and cyanamide self-reaction compete. This is the shortest terminal assembly step, not a claim that arginine will be the dominant product.

reactions.name: Hydration of argininonitrile to argininamide

conditions.other: Acidic water at approximately pH 1-3; guanidino group protonated; controlled thermal exposure.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-promoted nitrile hydration forms the primary amide while retaining the guanidino substituent.
reactions.reasoning: The functional-group transformation is established in general. Its useful rate and chemoselectivity on this substrate in a natural fluid remain speculative. Acidic conditions reduce nucleophilic side-chain reactions, but they do not guarantee quantitative guanidino-group survival.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of argininamide to arginine

conditions.other: Acidic aqueous compartment, approximately pH 1-3; cooling after hydrolysis to limit further decomposition.

reactions.mechanism: Carboxamide hydrolysis releases ammonia and produces the arginine carboxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: This uses ordinary amide hydrolysis rather than biological amidases. Arginine can survive some acidic hydrolysis conditions, but the balance between the required reaction time and substrate degradation must be established for the proposed fluid. No prebiotic yield is asserted.

reactions.name: Bucherer-Bergs capture of ornithinonitrile as a hydantoin

conditions.other: Ammonium-carbonate-containing water at pH approximately 8-10; sufficient dissolved inorganic carbon; shaded concentrated pool.

reactions.mechanism: Carbon dioxide capture by the alpha-amino group and subsequent cyclization and rearrangement give the hydantoin; this node represents the net Bucherer-Bergs conversion.
reactions.reasoning: Hydantoin formation through alpha-aminonitrile and inorganic-carbon chemistry is an established alternative to direct Strecker hydrolysis. Applying it selectively to this diamino substrate is speculative because the terminal amine also reacts and can promote cyclization. The hydantoin branch is included because it masks the alpha-amino group during later guanidination.

reactions.name: Guanidination of ornithine hydantoin

conditions.other: Concentrated cyanamide; mildly alkaline water, approximately pH 8.5-10; avoid extended strong-base exposure.

reactions.mechanism: The exocyclic primary amine adds to cyanamide, retaining the hydantoin ring as an alpha-amino-group mask.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative but chemically motivated: incorporation of the alpha nitrogen into a carbonyl-containing ring should reduce its competition with the terminal primary amine. Deprotonated hydantoin nitrogens may nevertheless react, and cyanamide self-condensation competes. Improved regioselectivity must be demonstrated rather than assumed.

reactions.name: Ring-opening hydrolysis of ornithine hydantoin

conditions.other: Alkaline water, approximately pH 10-11; prolonged residence may be necessary; subsequent cooling.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic cleavage of the hydantoin ring produces the N-alpha-carbamoyl amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Hydantoin ring opening is established chemistry, but laboratory procedures can require harsher conditions than a natural alkaline vent supplies. Therefore useful conversion in this temperature and pH window is speculative. Accumulation of the open-chain carbamoyl compound creates a distinct site-protected guanidination opportunity.

reactions.name: Guanidination of N-alpha-carbamoylornithine

conditions.other: Cooled, concentrated solution at pH approximately 9-10.5; alpha-carbamoyl group retained during cyanamide exposure.

reactions.mechanism: The free side-chain primary amine adds to cyanamide while the alpha nitrogen remains carbamoylated.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate application with a rational selectivity advantage: the carbamoylated alpha nitrogen is less nucleophilic than a free alpha amine. This avoids requiring cyanamide to discriminate between two unprotected primary amines. Carbamoyl stability and target-product selectivity under repeated concentration cycles remain unresolved.

reactions.name: Decarbamoylation to ornithine

conditions.other: Transfer from alkaline water to an acidic pore, approximately pH 1-3; sufficient residence for carbamoyl cleavage.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic cleavage of the N-carbamoyl group liberates ornithine; decomposition of the released carbamic-acid equivalent yields carbon dioxide and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Nonenzymatic removal of an N-carbamoyl group is chemically possible but often demanding. The proposed environmental rate is uncertain and may be too low before other degradation occurs. This completes the hydantoin route to ornithine without introducing a biological carbamoylase.

reactions.name: Bucherer-Bergs capture of argininonitrile

conditions.other: Ammonium-carbonate-containing solution at pH approximately 8-10; guanidino side chain mostly protonated.

reactions.mechanism: Carbon dioxide incorporation and cyclization of the alpha-aminonitrile generate the arginine-substituted hydantoin.
reactions.reasoning: This is a speculative substrate extension of established Bucherer-Bergs chemistry. A protonated guanidino group should compete less strongly than a free terminal amine, but neither hydantoin yield nor side-chain survival is established under the proposed prebiotic conditions. The incorporated carbon is subsequently released during decarbamoylation.

reactions.name: Ring-opening hydrolysis of arginine hydantoin

conditions.other: Alkaline water at approximately pH 10-11; thermal exposure minimized after ring opening.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis opens the hydantoin ring to N-alpha-carbamoylarginine.
reactions.reasoning: The ring-opening reaction class is established, but this substrate and geochemical operating window are speculative. A major selectivity problem is achieving hydantoin hydrolysis before guanidino-group hydrolysis or other decomposition. The graph does not assume that prolonged alkaline heating preserves arginine functionality.

reactions.name: Decarbamoylation to arginine

conditions.other: Acidic aqueous pore, approximately pH 1-3; cooling and dilution after target formation.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis removes the alpha-carbamoyl group, generating arginine, carbon dioxide and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as a selective prebiotic operation. Hydrolytic N-decarbamoylation is chemically grounded, but it must occur faster than damage to the side-chain guanidino group. No enzyme or modern protecting-group reagent is assumed. This selectivity and the required residence time are key unresolved constraints on every hydantoin-to-arginine branch.

pathways.name: C4 aminonitrile guanidination before aldehyde formation
pathways.description: Install the guanidino group on the C4 aminonitrile, partially reduce the remaining nitrile to an aldehyde, and complete Strecker extension followed by direct hydrolysis. This avoids guanidinating a molecule with two primary amines but requires unvalidated selective reduction of a guanidinated nitrile.

pathways.name: Aminoaldehyde guanidination followed by direct Strecker hydrolysis
pathways.description: Generate the aminoaldehyde, guanidinate its terminal amine, and then install and hydrolyze the alpha-aminonitrile. Competition between aminoaldehyde cyclization and guanidination is the distinguishing bottleneck.

pathways.name: Ornithinonitrile guanidination followed by direct hydrolysis
pathways.description: Perform Strecker extension before guanidination, then hydrolyze the guanidinated alpha-aminonitrile through argininamide. Side-chain versus alpha-amino guanidination is unresolved.

pathways.name: Ornithinamide-stage guanidination
pathways.description: Hydrate the ornithine precursor nitrile to its amide before guanidination, then hydrolyze argininamide. This changes the competing nitrile chemistry but still requires regioselective guanidination of an unprotected diamino compound.

pathways.name: Direct Strecker synthesis of ornithine followed by guanidination
pathways.description: Complete nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis before adding the guanidino group. This avoids exposing an already formed guanidino group to the initial hydrolysis sequence but leaves terminal guanidination selectivity unresolved.

pathways.name: Aminoaldehyde guanidination followed by the arginine hydantoin branch
pathways.description: Guanidinate before Strecker extension, trap the resulting alpha-aminonitrile as a hydantoin, and hydrolyze through N-alpha-carbamoylarginine. This substitutes a cyclic intermediate for direct nitrile-to-amide hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Ornithinonitrile guanidination followed by hydantoin formation
pathways.description: Guanidinate the Strecker-derived diamino nitrile before carbon dioxide capture and hydantoin formation. This requires both guanidination regioselectivity and guanidino-group survival through hydantoin processing.

pathways.name: Hydantoin-masked guanidination
pathways.description: Convert ornithinonitrile to ornithine hydantoin before guanidination. The ring masks the alpha nitrogen and may improve side-chain selectivity; subsequent hydrolysis must preserve the newly installed guanidino group.

pathways.name: Open-chain N-alpha-carbamoyl-masked guanidination
pathways.description: Open ornithine hydantoin before guanidination, retaining the alpha-carbamoyl group as a temporary selectivity aid. Guanidination is followed only by decarbamoylation, avoiding alkaline hydantoin opening after guanidino-group installation.

pathways.name: Hydantoin route to ornithine followed by terminal guanidination
pathways.description: Fully hydrolyze and decarbamoylate the ornithine hydantoin branch before guanidination. This avoids guanidino-group exposure to hydantoin-processing conditions but sacrifices the alpha-nitrogen masking advantage during the final reaction.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest conditional design: early guanidination avoids competition between alpha and side-chain amino groups and may suppress the cyclization associated with an unprotected aminoaldehyde. Nevertheless, rxn_003 and rxn_006 require two different, unestablished hydrogenation selectivities. An unspecified hydrothermal catalyst cannot be assumed to stop at the required aminonitrile or aldehyde. The subsequent Strecker and hydrolysis sequence is formally credible, but production of its aldehyde substrate and survival of the guanidino group remain undemonstrated.
suggestions: Identify a naturally available catalyst and measure rxn_003 and rxn_006 under specified H2 pressure, pH, temperature and residence time, including over-reduced and cyclic products.
Demonstrate rxn_005 before substantial aminonitrile cyclization or cyanamide hydration and oligomerization.
Validate the complete sequence through rxn_016, including cooling and transfer conditions, with structural confirmation of arginine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Guanidination before introducing the alpha-amino group avoids a later two-amine regioselectivity problem. However, rxn_004 must produce 4-aminobutanal without over-reduction, and rxn_007 must capture it despite favorable five-membered cyclic imine formation. Cyanamide guanidination cannot be assumed to outcompete this intramolecular reaction. The guanidinated-aldehyde Strecker sequence is reasonable in principle, but its precursor supply remains unsupported.
suggestions: Measure open-chain 4-aminobutanal, cyclic imine and over-reduction products under the actual rxn_004 conditions.
Establish a pH and concentration window in which rxn_007 outcompetes aminoaldehyde cyclization and cyanamide side reactions.
Test the guanidinated aldehyde through Strecker conversion and hydrolysis without assuming intermediate survival during transfer.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Besides the speculative reductions, rxn_008 must favor intermolecular Strecker chemistry over aminoaldehyde cyclization. Cyanide capture of the resulting cyclic imine can instead lead toward prolinenitrile. Rxn_010 then requires side-chain-selective guanidination of an unprotected diamino substrate; neither the molecular formula nor the balanced equation establishes that selectivity. The final hydrolyses are recognizable transformations, but they cannot correct an incorrectly cyclized or guanidinated precursor.
suggestions: Quantify ornithinonitrile versus cyclic Strecker products across realistic ammonia concentration and pH ranges.
Resolve alpha-, side-chain- and bis-guanidinated products using structure-sensitive analysis rather than formula or mass alone.
Demonstrate the selective reductions before treating downstream guanidination and hydrolysis as an accessible route.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydration to ornithinamide is chemically plausible, but it does not protect the alpha-amino group. Rxn_012 therefore still requires experimentally demonstrated side-chain selectivity. Accumulating the amide for guanidination also requires control over continued hydrolysis and competing cyclization. The common rxn_003/rxn_004 reduction bottleneck and rxn_008 aminoaldehyde competition remain unresolved, so this is a formal route rather than an established source of arginine.
suggestions: Measure whether ornithinamide accumulates under the proposed hydration conditions and remains available during subsequent transfer.
Determine the guanidination product distribution of ornithinamide under explicitly specified cyanamide conditions.
Verify that rxn_016 preserves the desired guanidino functionality while converting the amide to arginine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The aminonitrile-to-ornithine hydrolysis sequence is conventional in outline. Its accessibility is nevertheless limited by rxn_003, rxn_004 and competition with cyclic products in rxn_008. Terminal cyanamide guanidination of unprotected ornithine is not automatically selective for the side-chain amino group. The final equation identifies the intended product but provides no evidence distinguishing arginine from alternative guanidination products.
suggestions: Demonstrate ornithine formation and quantify cyclic or degraded products under the complete Strecker-hydrolysis conditions.
Establish side-chain-selective cyanamide guanidination without enzymes or modern protecting and activating reagents.
Confirm the terminal product structurally and report its yield relative to alternative guanidinated ornithine isomers.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Bucherer-Bergs capture is a plausible reaction-family extension, provided suitable aqueous CO2, ammonia and carbonate speciation is established. It does not solve the earlier selective reductions or the need for rxn_007 to outcompete aminoaldehyde cyclization. Because guanidination has already occurred, the hydantoin is not providing selectivity during that step. Nonenzymatic ring opening and decarbamoylation must be shown to release arginine while retaining its guanidino group.
suggestions: Specify and test the pH, dissolved inorganic carbon, ammonia concentration and temperature for rxn_022.
Demonstrate rxn_023 and rxn_024 using geochemically defensible acid or base conditions, with simultaneous measurements of arginine and degradation products.
Resolve the aminoaldehyde production and guanidination bottlenecks independently of the downstream hydantoin chemistry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydantoin formation occurs after guanidination, so it cannot prevent or correct wrong-site guanidination in rxn_010. This pathway retains the speculative nitrile reductions, cyclic-imine competition during rxn_008 and unprotected diamine selectivity problem. The hydantoin branch is formally balanced and chemically recognizable, but its ring-opening and decarbamoylation conditions are unspecified and target recovery is unverified.
suggestions: Establish the structure and regioisomeric purity of argininonitrile before testing hydantoin formation.
Measure hydantoin conversion and subsequent arginine recovery under a fully specified, nonenzymatic condition sequence.
Compare guanidination before and after alpha-amino masking experimentally rather than assuming later hydantoin formation resolves earlier selectivity.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway has a sound late-stage selectivity rationale: hydantoin formation reduces alpha-amino nucleophilicity before side-chain guanidination. That is a chemical advantage, not experimental proof of selectivity. Rxn_017 must give the intended hydantoin despite the additional amino group, and rxn_023/rxn_024 must subsequently recover arginine. Most importantly, masking does not bypass rxn_003/rxn_004 or the competition between open-chain and cyclic Strecker chemistry in rxn_008.
suggestions: Demonstrate ornithine hydantoin formation under specified ammonia/CO2 conditions and identify competing cyclic or carbamoylated products.
Measure side-chain versus hydantoin-nitrogen guanidination and the stability of the mask under rxn_018 conditions.
Validate nonenzymatic deprotection through rxn_024 while separately establishing the upstream selective reductions and ornithinonitrile formation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: An N-alpha-carbamoyl group plausibly reduces alpha-nitrogen reactivity and improves the rationale for side-chain guanidination. However, rxn_019 must accumulate the intended open-chain intermediate, and that mask must survive rxn_020 without substantial reclosure or premature removal. Final decarbamoylation to arginine remains condition-dependent and unverified. The shared selective reductions and aminoaldehyde cyclization problem are unchanged.
suggestions: Confirm the identity and accumulation of N-alpha-carbamoylornithine during hydantoin ring opening.
Measure mask retention, hydantoin reclosure and guanidination regioselectivity under rxn_020 conditions.
Establish a nonenzymatic decarbamoylation window that releases arginine faster than competing decomposition.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The hydantoin branch provides a formally valid route to ornithine, but removing the alpha-amino mask before rxn_014 forfeits its potential benefit for guanidination selectivity. Terminal guanidination therefore has the same unresolved two-amine problem as P5. Nonenzymatic hydantoin opening and decarbamoylation also require demonstrated conditions. None of these transformations bypasses the speculative reductions or competing cyclic chemistry before ornithinonitrile formation.
suggestions: Demonstrate ornithine recovery through rxn_019 and rxn_021 under realistic hydrothermal pH and residence times.
Quantify side-chain-selective guanidination of the recovered ornithine, including alternative constitutional isomers.
Compare terminal guanidination with guanidination while the alpha-amino mask remains present; retain only strategies supported by measured selectivity.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network has strong structural validity: it contains sufficient nodes, is connected, uses molecule IDs consistently and provides formal routes to arginine. The supplied deterministic balance check is accepted as ground truth. There are no conservation violations; rxn_003 requires 2 H2, a reasonable stoichiometric correction. Carbon and nitrogen accounting is coherent. Chemical viability is much weaker. Every target route requires rxn_003 followed by either rxn_004 or rxn_006, and none has a demonstrated geochemical catalyst and operating window for the required selectivity. Over-reduction and cyclization are substantial alternatives. Routes through free 4-aminobutanal additionally face cyclic-imine formation, while unmasked guanidination routes require unresolved positional selectivity. Hydantoin and carbamoyl masking are chemically motivated but do not establish upstream precursor production or successful nonenzymatic deprotection. Environmental scores reflect missing reaction-specific information: temperature, pH, H2 pressure, catalyst identity and availability, residence time, and physically justified cooling and transfer. A copper-catalyst label does not establish an active natural copper phase or suitable cyanide speciation. No penalty is assigned for the number or ordering of environments. Starting supplies are accepted as stipulated, and racemic arginine satisfies the stated target. The explicit acknowledgment of speculation is appropriate but does not substitute for evidence. No research findings were supplied for a separate literature-alignment assessment. P1 is the best conditional design because it avoids unprotected aminoaldehyde handling and later two-amine guanidination, not because its key reductions are established. Confidence is bottleneck-weighted rather than an average of reaction scores. The complete network is not approved.
